title: Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive support
summary: Learn how Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive are wired together in Microsoft 365, then support the everyday tickets: file sync errors, lost files, sharing problems, and guest access.
objectives: Explain how a Team is backed by a Microsoft 365 group and a SharePoint site, and where Teams files actually live
Navigate the Teams admin center to find policies, meeting policies, and external/guest access settings
Manage SharePoint sites, document libraries, and internal versus external sharing links
Support OneDrive for Business: the sync client, Known Folder Move, and storage quotas
Resolve common tickets: file sync errors, restoring a lost file, and access problems
Recognise retention and orphaned-site issues that follow when a Team or group is deleted

quiz.q: Where do files shared in a Microsoft Teams channel actually get stored?
options: In a SharePoint document library on the team's site
quiz.why: Each standard channel maps to a folder in the **Documents** library of the team's backing SharePoint site, so Teams files are really SharePoint files.

quiz.q: When you create a new Team, what is automatically created alongside it?
options: A Microsoft 365 group and a SharePoint site
quiz.why: A Team is backed by a **Microsoft 365 group**, which provisions a SharePoint site, a group mailbox, a calendar, and a Planner — delete the group and all of these go with it.

quiz.q: A user deleted a file from a SharePoint document library yesterday. Where do you look first to restore it?
quiz.why: Deleted items go to the **site Recycle Bin** for 93 days; if it was emptied there, the **second-stage Recycle Bin** is the next stop before any tenant-level recovery.

quiz.q: Which feature automatically redirects a user's Desktop, Documents, and Pictures folders into OneDrive?
quiz.why: **Known Folder Move (KFM)** redirects the Windows known folders into OneDrive so they sync and survive a device loss; Files On-Demand is separate and controls local availability.

quiz.q: An external partner cannot open a file a colleague 'shared' with them. List two settings you would check.
quiz.answer: Check the SharePoint/OneDrive external sharing level for the tenant and that specific site (it may be set to internal-only), and check the sharing link type used (a 'People in your organisation' link will not work for guests — they need a 'Specific people' or 'Anyone' link).
quiz.why: Sharing fails most often because the site or tenant external-sharing policy blocks it, or because the wrong **link type** was chosen — both must allow the external recipient.

quiz.q: Why can deleting a Team or its Microsoft 365 group cause an 'orphaned' SharePoint site, and what is the retention concern?
quiz.answer: Deleting the group deletes its connected SharePoint site, mailbox, and Teams content together; if a retention policy is applied, content may be preserved in a hidden/preservation state even after deletion, and admins can restore the group (and its site) within the 30-day soft-delete window.
quiz.why: Group-connected resources share a lifecycle, so **retention** and the **30-day soft delete** window govern whether content can be recovered before it is permanently purged.

body_markdown:
## How Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive fit together

This is the single most important idea in the lesson: these three services are one connected system. When you create a **Team**, Microsoft 365 quietly provisions a **Microsoft 365 group** behind it. That group brings a **SharePoint site**, a group mailbox, a calendar, and a Planner. Every file someone drops into a Teams channel is actually stored in the **Documents** library of that SharePoint site — Teams is just a friendly front door to SharePoint.

**OneDrive for Business** is the personal version of the same SharePoint storage engine: each user gets their own site for private files. Files shared in a one-to-one or group **chat** (not a channel) live in the sender's OneDrive, not the team site. Knowing where a file physically lives tells you exactly which admin center to open when a ticket lands.

## The Teams admin center

Most Teams tickets are solved with **policies**. Open the Teams admin center to manage them.

```text
admin.teams.microsoft.com
  -> Teams -> Manage teams        (find and own a team)
  -> Meetings -> Meeting policies (recording, lobby, sharing)
  -> Users -> Guest access        (allow/block external guests)
  -> Org-wide settings -> External access
```

**External access** (federation) lets your users chat with people in other Microsoft 365 organisations. **Guest access** lets you add an outside person directly into a team as a guest. They are different switches, and tickets like "I can't add my client to the team" usually trace back to one of them being off.

## SharePoint sites, libraries and sharing

In the SharePoint admin center you manage every site, including the ones created by Teams. The key support concept is **sharing**.

```text
admin.microsoft.com -> SharePoint admin center
  -> Sites -> Active sites        (every site + storage used)
  -> Policies -> Sharing          (tenant external-sharing level)
```

Sharing has two layers. The **tenant** sets the maximum (for example, "Anyone", "New and existing guests", or "Only people in your organisation"), and each **site** can be set equal or more restrictive — never more permissive than the tenant. When someone clicks **Share**, the **link type** matters: a *People in your organisation* link will never work for an external guest. Sharing tickets are almost always a policy level or a wrong link type.

You can also drive this with the SharePoint Online Management Shell:

```powershell
Connect-SPOService -Url https://contoso-admin.sharepoint.com
Get-SPOSite -Limit All | Select Url, Owner, StorageUsageCurrent
Get-SPOSite -Identity https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Sales | Select SharingCapability
```

## OneDrive and the sync client

The **OneDrive sync client** keeps files mirrored between the PC and the cloud. **Known Folder Move (KFM)** redirects the Desktop, Documents, and Pictures folders into OneDrive so they sync automatically and survive a lost laptop. **Files On-Demand** keeps files cloud-only until opened, saving disk space. When sync stalls, check the blue/grey cloud icons, look for a paused client, an over-quota account, or a filename with illegal characters.

## Common tickets and how you fix them

- **"I lost a file."** Check **version history** first (restore an earlier version), then the **site Recycle Bin** (93 days), then the second-stage Recycle Bin.
- **File sync error.** Reset or restart the sync client, confirm the user is signed in, check storage quota, and rename files with `\ / : * ? " < > |`.
- **Can't access a site or team.** Confirm group membership — access follows the **Microsoft 365 group**, not a one-off permission.
- **Sharing not working.** Check tenant and site external-sharing level, then the link type.
- **Orphaned sites and retention.** Deleting a Team deletes its group and SharePoint site together. A **retention policy** may preserve content even after deletion, and a deleted group can be restored within **30 days**.

## Your task

In a test tenant or lab, create a Team, find its backing SharePoint site in the SharePoint admin center, upload a file to a channel, delete it, and restore it from the site Recycle Bin. Then connect with `Connect-SPOService` and run `Get-SPOSite` to list your sites and their sharing capability.

slides.title: Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive support
slides.narration: Welcome to Lesson Four of Month Six. Today we tie together the three services you'll touch most as a Tier Two cloud admin: Teams, SharePoint, and OneDrive. The big secret is that they're really one connected system, and once you understand how they're wired, the everyday tickets — sync errors, lost files, sharing problems, guest access — all start to make sense. This is core MS dash one oh two material, so let's get into it.

slides.title: One connected system
bullets: A Team is backed by a Microsoft 365 group.
The group provisions a SharePoint site automatically.
Teams channel files live in that SharePoint site.
OneDrive is the same engine, for personal files.
slides.narration: Here's the single most important idea. When you create a Team, Microsoft 365 quietly creates a Microsoft 365 group behind it. That group brings a SharePoint site, a group mailbox, a calendar, and a Planner. Every file someone drops into a Teams channel is actually stored in a document library on that SharePoint site. Teams is just a friendly front door to SharePoint. And OneDrive for Business is the very same storage engine, just the personal version, one site per user.

slides.title: Where does a file actually live?
bullets: Channel files -> the team's SharePoint site.
Chat files -> the sender's OneDrive.
Knowing the location tells you which admin center.
This drives almost every support decision.
slides.narration: Follow the file. If someone shares a file in a channel, it lives in the team's SharePoint site. If they share it in a one-to-one or group chat — not a channel — it lives in the sender's OneDrive instead. This matters enormously for support, because knowing where a file physically lives tells you exactly which admin center to open and where to go looking when the ticket lands on your desk.

Meeting policies: recording, lobby, sharing.

Meeting policies control things like recording, the lobby, and screen sharing. And tucked away you'll find guest access and external access — write those two down, because we'll separate them on the next slide.

slides.title: Guest access vs external access
bullets: External access: chat with other M365 orgs (federation).
Guest access: add an outsider into your team as a guest.
They are two different switches.

slides.narration: These two get confused constantly. External access, sometimes called federation, lets your users chat with people in other Microsoft 365 organisations. Guest access is different: it lets you add an outside person directly into one of your teams as a guest, so they can see channels and files. They're two separate switches. So when a ticket says I can't add my client to the team, it almost always traces back to one of these being switched off.

slides.narration: In the SharePoint admin center you manage every site, including the ones Teams created. Sharing has two layers. The tenant sets the maximum — for example Anyone, or New and existing guests, or Only people in your organisation. Each individual site can be equal to that or more restrictive, but never more permissive than the tenant. And when a user clicks Share, the link type matters: a People in your organisation link will never work for an outside guest.

Get-SPOSite lists sites, owners and storage used.

slides.narration: For bulk work, reach for the SharePoint Online Management Shell. You connect with Connect dash S P O Service, pointing at your admin U R L. Then Get dash S P O Site lists every site with its owner and the storage it's using. You can also pull the SharingCapability on a single site to confirm whether external sharing is allowed there. It's far faster than clicking through hundreds of sites by hand.

slides.narration: Let's recap. A Team is backed by a Microsoft 365 group plus a SharePoint site, and channel files live in SharePoint. Sharing has two layers, the tenant maximum and the per-site setting. OneDrive gives each user personal storage with the sync client, Known Folder Move, and Files On-Demand. And remember, deleting a group deletes its site too, so keep retention and the thirty-day restore window in mind to avoid orphaned content.
